children.value: The five questionnaires of the core battery (STICSA trait, STICSA state, BDI-II, OCI, IUS) correlate .41–.78. This chapter summarises them by one general factor and tests that factor with the questionnaire models of RQ2 and RQ3, the structure analyses, the placement strategies and the hybrid switch model. All numbers refer to run 13_11. Slopes are per SD of the score. Event indicators are tested with logistic GEE clustered by participant (log-odds); participant-level measures with OLS and HC3 standard errors. Condition is included as a covariate (contrasts Full vs None + Partial, Partial vs None), and slopes within conditions come from the model with the score × condition interaction.

1  Scale factor in the task sample

children.value: One-factor CFA of the z-scored totals (lavaan, MLR, FIML; N = 85):
Standardised loadings: STICSA trait .92, BDI .84, STICSA state .84, OCI .69, IUS .59.
Parallel analysis indicates one factor (eigenvalues 3.43, 0.68, …), which carries 69 % of the variance; ω_total = .89.
Fit: CFI .95, SRMR .047, RMSEA .175. A residual covariance between STICSA state and trait does not improve the fit.
The regression factor score correlates .98 with the mean of the z-scored totals.
2  Item level in the task sample

children.label: 2  Item level in the task sample

children.value: Minres EFA on smoothed Pearson correlations of the items (N = 84), for the five questionnaires (93 items) and all ten questionnaires (188 items, adding PCL-5, ACE, SIAS, ERS, EAT-26). Solutions: one factor; the general factor of a Schmid–Leiman bifactor solution with one group factor per questionnaire; five oblimin factors (ten Berge scores).

Five questionnaires: the first eigenvalue explains 24 % of the variance; ω_h = .60, explained common variance (ECV) of the general factor .36. The five oblimin factors are roughly BDI, IUS, STICSA cognitive, STICSA somatic, and OCI with somatic items.

Ten questionnaires: ω_h = .59, ECV .24. The five oblimin factors are general distress (STICSA, BDI, OCI), ERS, PCL/ACE/somatic, SIAS and EAT. ACE and EAT load weakly on the general factor (mean .15–.20).
With more items than participants, the item structure is not reproducible: loadings estimated in two random halves of the sample correlate .41–.47.
The item-level general scores correlate .98 (five questionnaires) and .93–.94 (ten) with the scale factor.

Agglomerative clustering of the items (distance 1 − r; average linkage, Ward’s method, ICLUST). Stability of the item partitions for 2–10 clusters, as the adjusted Rand index (ARI) between two random halves of the participants: Ward .10–.18, EFA .12–.18 (five questionnaires); .12–.17 for both (ten questionnaires). Average linkage merges almost all items into one cluster. At this N, no item partition is reproducible; only the top splits are interpretable (Ward, five questionnaires, two clusters: STICSA + BDI + half of OCI + 5 IUS items vs most of IUS + half of OCI).

For the IRT models, response categories chosen by fewer than 5 % of respondents are merged with the neighbouring category. Loading-weighted sums are used for the item EFA and Schmid–Leiman scores because regression weights are unstable with more items than respondents.

Parcel bifactor: CFI .932, TLI .905, RMSEA .120, SRMR .045; ω_h = .90, ECV of G .69. Loadings on G: STICSA trait .77–.92, STICSA state .70–.89, BDI .78–.80, IUS .63–.70, OCI .66–.69. OCI and IUS keep the largest specific variance (specific loadings .55–.65).
IRT graded response: mean discrimination 1.18 (OCI) to 1.41 (BDI); M2-based CFI .90, RMSEA .089.

Correlation of the Schmid–Leiman score (weights from the 77 respondents without task data) with the subscales in the task sample: STICSA trait cognitive .88, STICSA state cognitive .83, BDI .86, OCI obsessing .77, IUS inhibitory .77, STICSA trait somatic .67, IUS prospective .61, STICSA state somatic .60, OCI ordering .59, OCI checking .42, OCI washing .39.

Split-half: the model fitted in two random halves of the 161 respondents (50 times; IRT models 15 times), both fits used to score all respondents, and the two scores correlated. Out-of-sample: the model fitted in the 77 respondents without task data, the task participants scored with these weights, and the scores correlated with those of the fit in all 161.

The hybrid switch model describes a participant as a direction tracker that switches, at trial tau, to latent-state inference, on which it relies with weight w after the switch; both systems make the same non-structural responses (exact repeats, following a surprising attack, split placements, lapses).
